issues.legal_issue: A transfer of a tenant’s interest in premises may create a deemed vacancy for requisition even when the transfer is permitted under rent-control law.
material_facts: A tenant assigned her interest in the premises to the petitioners as part of a stated transfer of a business as a going concern.
The State requisitioned the premises for a public purpose after treating the assignment as creating a vacancy.
issues.conclusion: The assignment could be treated as creating a deemed vacancy under the requisition law, notwithstanding that it might be permitted under the rent law, and the State could requisition the premises on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 and Explanation (a) of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 treat premises as vacant when a tenant assigns or transfers an interest in them. Section 15(1) and the notification issued under its proviso concern the legality of tenancy transfers under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947; they are not read into section 6. The two Acts address different subject matters and are not in pari materia. The Court acknowledged the general principle of construing related provisions harmoniously where possible, including the principle discussed in Kedar Nath Singh v. State of Bihar, but held it inapplicable to these distinct Acts.

predicates.requisition_case: The government sought to requisition premises under a law governing requisition of property.
predicates.tenant_transferred_interest: A tenant assigned or otherwise transferred an interest in the premises to another person.
predicates.premises_sought_for_public_purpose: The government sought the premises for a public purpose.

issues.definition: When the government seeks premises for a public purpose in a requisition proceeding and a tenant has transferred an interest in them, the transfer creates a deemed vacancy on which requisition may proceed.

issues.legal_issue: A law governing requisition of property does not, by that fact alone, regulate the freedom to carry on trade or business.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged the requisition law as infringing the constitutional freedom to carry on trade or business.
The Court found that the law dealt with property and not trade or business as such.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional challenge to the requisition law under the freedom to carry on trade or business did not arise for consideration, although a particular requisition order might interfere with a person’s ability to do business.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed the scope and operation of the Bombay Land Requisition Act, 1948 and held that it regulates property, not trade or business as such. It therefore did not decide whether a particular requisition order might interfere with the ability to conduct business.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_requisition_: A party challenged a law governing requisition of property as infringing the freedom to carry on trade or business.
predicates.law_confined_to_property: The challenged law governs property and does not regulate trade or business as such.

issues.definition: A challenge to a requisition law does not engage the freedom to carry on trade or business when the law governs property and not trade or business.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot establish infringement of constitutional rights through requisition by relying on a purported going-concern transfer that is in substance a prohibited transfer of tenancy rights.
material_facts: The deed described a transfer of a shoe business as a going concern together with the tenancy rights, but no cash consideration was paid for the tenancy rights.
The petitioners carried on a different business in the premises from the shoe business described in the deed.
The Court found the arrangement to be a colourable device to obtain a tenancy transfer otherwise prohibited by the rent law, and found that the notification did not protect it.
The petitioners relied on the deed to claim tenancy and business rights and to allege infringement of their constitutional rights to property and to carry on business.
issues.conclusion: The purported assignment did not give the petitioners rights in the tenancy or to carry on business in the premises; they therefore could not establish infringement of their constitutional rights to property or to carry on business, and the petition failed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 prohibits a tenant from assigning or transferring an interest in premises except as permitted. Clause 2 of the notification under the proviso to section 15(1) protects a transfer incidental to a genuine sale of an entire business as a going concern together with its stock-in-trade and goodwill. A transaction that is in substance a device to transfer tenancy rights outside that permission does not confer the claimed tenancy or business rights. The Court accordingly found no infringement of the constitutional rights under Articles 19(1)(f) and 19(1)(g). It did not decide the separate argument concerning Article 31(2) or the applicability or reconsideration of Sitabati Devi v. State of West Bengal.

rule.if: constitutional_rights_challenge_to_requisition and purported_going_concern_transfer and recipient_operated_different_business and tenancy_transfer_not_protected

predicates.constitutional_rights_challenge_to_requi: A party challenged a requisition as infringing constitutional rights to property or to carry on business.
predicates.purported_going_concern_transfer: The transfer document described the tenancy as incidental to a transfer of a business as a going concern.
predicates.recipient_operated_different_business: The recipient carried on a business different from the business described as transferred.
predicates.tenancy_transfer_not_protected: The transaction was in substance a tenancy transfer outside the permitted category of genuine business transfers.

issues.definition: When a party challenges requisition based on a purported going-concern transfer, but the recipient operated a different business and the tenancy transfer was not protected, the party cannot establish infringement of fundamental rights through the claimed transfer.
